logline: Seven superhuman adoptees reunite at their eccentric father's death to prevent an apocalypse - and can barely stand each other.

bollymeter.basis: 77% RT; critics found the tone and ensemble appealing but the plotting messy. Audiences embraced the show's anarchic energy and the chemistry of the Hargreeves siblings, particularly Aidan Gallagher's Number Five.

pull_quotes.text: An imaginative, irreverent superhero series that works better when focused on its endearing ensemble than its chaotic plot.

seasons.review_body: The Umbrella Academy Season 1 is the messy, charming debut of a show that works better as a vibe than as a plot machine. The Gerard Way comic's core idea - superheroes as a dysfunctional family unit rather than a assembled team - gives the writers a distinct emotional frame. The sibling dynamics, especially the fractured relationship between Luther and Diego and Allison, have genuine texture. Aidan Gallagher as Number Five is the standout: a 58-year-old assassin trapped in a 13-year-old's body, he commands every scene with an old-soul authority that should not work but does completely. The apocalypse-prevention plot is serviceable at best. Critics at 77% were right to note the structural looseness, but the audience's affection (8.0 IMDb) captures something the numbers miss: this show is genuinely fun to be in.

bollymeter.basis: 91% RT - the show's critical summit. The 1960s Dallas setting gave the ensemble structure the first season lacked; critics found the tighter scenario and stronger character work a genuine upgrade.

pull_quotes.text: A substantial improvement - more focused, more emotional, and funnier, with a 1960s setting that unlocks the show's full potential.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 is the Umbrella Academy at its best: the 1960s Dallas setting functions as narrative constraint in the best possible way, forcing the scattered siblings into a tighter geography and a tighter story. The civil rights backdrop gives Allison's arc real weight. Klaus's cult storyline is the season's comedic high point. The Commission sequences and the Handler's return are vintage comic-book television - stylised and propulsive. Critics at 91% recognised the improvement comprehensively: this is a sharper, more confident version of the show, with the ensemble dynamics calibrated and the time-travel mechanics now in service of character rather than plot complication. The Sparrow Academy reveal is Season 2's best cliffhanger.

episode_reviews.title: Right Back Where We Started
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The siblings scatter across 1963 Dallas after Five's botched time jump. The 1960s setting immediately gives the show a structural clarity and visual identity that Season 1 lacked. Each character's solo situation is funny and purposeful - the episode is breezy, confident, and better than anything in the first season.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The opening montage of each sibling landing in 1963 and immediately causing havoc - the show finding its comic timing.

critic_note.text: A substantial improvement - more focused, more emotional, and funnier, with a 1960s setting that unlocks the show's full potential.

episode_reviews.title: The Majestic 12
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The season's conspiracy thriller layer thickens as The Commission and the Umbrella Academy both manoeuvre for the same information. Allison's civil rights arc reaches a turning point; Five's corporate-espionage subplot delivers the season's best comedic setpiece.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Five's briefcase negotiation with the Handler - one of Aidan Gallagher's best scenes, playing an old man's cunning in a teenager's body.

episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The penultimate episode assembles the season's pieces with mounting urgency. The Sparrow Academy timeline is introduced as a consequence of the siblings' presence in the 1960s - a cliffhanger that retroactively makes the whole season feel like careful setup.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The timeline divergence reveal - the show demonstrating that it had been planning its finale from the first episode.

episode_reviews.title: The End of Something
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The season finale averts the apocalypse (again), introduces the Sparrow Academy, and ends on the show's boldest cliffhanger. The Hargreeves family dynamic has been genuinely enriched across the season; the ending rewards the investment.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The Sparrow Academy reveal - the shot that makes Season 3 instantly essential.

critic_note.text: The Umbrella Academy Season 2 ends with one of streaming television's most exciting cliffhangers in years.

seasons.season_over_season: A decisive step up from Season 1 in structure and character work; the 91% RT reflects a show that found itself.

bollymeter.basis: 91% RT - matched Season 2's critical score; the Sparrow Academy rivalry and the Hotel Oblivion arc landed well. Critics praised the season as continuation of the show's confident middle period.

pull_quotes.text: The Umbrella Academy maintains its winning formula - chaotic, emotional, wildly entertaining - with a new ensemble rivalry that adds fresh energy.

seasons.review_body: Season 3 has the structural confidence of a show that knows its own physics. The Sparrow Academy as rival sibling-unit works - the mirroring dynamic gives writers twice the dysfunction to play with. Sloane and Luther's romance is the season's emotional centre; the Hotel Oblivion sequences are ambitious. The audience score's slide (7.4 IMDb) relative to the critic consensus (91%) suggests diminishing returns for some viewers even while the show maintains its craft. The finale's universe reset - resetting character genders and relations - was polarising, and some fans found it thematically unearned. As a mid-series chapter with genuine highs and an uncertain ending, Season 3 sits exactly where it should: entertaining, slightly frustrating, never dull.
seasons.season_over_season: Lateral move from Season 2; strong in its midsection, divisive in its conclusion.

bollymeter.basis: 55% RT and 18% audience score - the show's lowest marks. Netflix's decision to limit the final season to six episodes left too many arcs unresolved; critics noted the rushed pacing and unsatisfying character conclusions.

pull_quotes.text: A truncated final season that squanders the goodwill of three earlier chapters with rushed resolutions and too many questions left unanswered.

seasons.review_body: Season 4 is the wrong kind of final season: compressed, uncertain, and clearly working under budget and episode constraints that hobble the storytelling. Six episodes to wrap four seasons of mythology - Netflix's decision, not the creators' - results in character arcs that snap shut rather than close. The Hotel Oblivion thread from Season 3 gets partial resolution at best. Individual performances remain committed; the cast never checked out. But the structural problems are too severe to overlook. A 55% RT and 18% audience score tell the story plainly: Season 4 did not give this ensemble the ending it had earned over three seasons. A disappointing conclusion to a show that, at its peak in Seasons 2 and 3, was genuinely lovable.
seasons.season_over_season: The weakest season by significant margin; the truncated episode count is the primary culprit.
